newsitem.title: USA: California investigators probe deaths of 39 men.
newsitem.headline: California investigators probe deaths of 39 men.

text.p: The bodies of 39 men, dressed alike and lying on mattresses or cots, were found scattered through a million-dollar California mansion on Wednesday in what appeared to be a mass suicide.
"Our initial reaction is that it was a suicide, but we are not ruling anything out," said Commander Alan Fulmer of the San Diego County Sheriff's Department.
But he said there was no immediate indication the men belonged to any religious cult.
The facts that there was no sign of blood or trauma and the positions of the bodies led police toward the suicide theory, Fulmer said. However, no suicide notes had been found.

He told reporters outside the sprawling mansion in the exclusive San Diego suburb of Rancho Santa Fe that the bodies were found by two Sheriff's deputies, who responded in the afternoon to an anonymous telephone tip.

"They discovered 39 deceased persons in different rooms," said Fulmer. "They were all in a prone position, on their backs with their arms by their sides and all appeared as if they had fallen asleep.".

All the men appeared to be 18-24 years old and white, although some of them might be Hispanic, he said. They were all wearing black trousers and black tennis shoes and were lying on either beds, mattresses or cots. There were no children among the dead and no survivors.
"We have no idea of their identities or where they come from," he said. "We don't know if they belonged to any religious cult or group or anything like that."

His comment was in response to a reporter's question suggesting a link to an incident in Quebec last Saturday, when five members of a doomsday cult -- the Solar Temple -- died in a blazing house in an apparent ritual suicide pact.
In 1994 and 1995, 69 members of the Solar Temple cult died in fires in Canada and Switzerland.
Fulmer said that after deputies discovered the bodies, they secured the house, which is valued at around $1.6 million and has a pool and a tennis court.
It is surrounded by a brick wall in a community of palatial estates known as "the Beverly Hills of San Diego" some 20 miles (32 km) north of the port city.
Investigators were trying to get a search warrant to go back in the house, he said, and the bodies would remain there while the investigation continued throughout the night.
Fulmer said the deputies who found the corpses "did a pretty thorough search" of the house and whether there were any more bodies in the house was "pure speculation."

A hazardous materials unit was examining the house to find the source of a "noxious, pungent odour," Fulmer said, adding that the first deputy in the house had worn a surgical mask and both deputies were taken to a local hospital for a precautionary check-up.
Fulmer said the house had been rented out since last October, but that the owner had not been located.
A neighbour, Bill Strong, told reporters the mansion was owned by a man named Sam Koutchessahani, who had rented it to people "from out of state" in October.
He said the people who lived in the house were "middle-aged, men and women." He had waved at them, but had no conversations.
Strong also said he had seen several vans at the house over the weekend and there were more people around.
Real estate agent Scott Warren, who said he showed the house recently, described to ABC's "Nightline" a "bizarre" scene in which the occupants considered the residence a "temple."

Both Warren and a couple who saw the house said in the report that a tall man in his 50s or 60s with gray hair met them at the door. One of those who saw the house said she was told the group represented themselves as "a self-sufficient religion" that rents houses around the country.
Warren said the occupants made him and his clients take off their shoes and put on slippers upon entering the house.

Warren said the bedrooms contained bunk beds and reminded him of a dormitory. He also said there was a main computer room in the back of the living area, and several people were seen in bedrooms working on computers "constantly."
Warren said those inside were dressed casually, but not necessarily in similar outfits.
"We just thought they were pretty bizarre," said Warren. "They were very strange in the way they were acting ... Constantly talking about brothers and sisters."
